# Cross-Compilation for Multiple Platforms

**Goal:** Master native cross-compilation in Nixpkgs, cross-compiling C/C++, Rust, and Go binaries from an `x86_64-linux` host to `aarch64-linux` (ARM64) and `riscv64-linux` targets without resorting to slow QEMU emulation, distinguishing `buildPlatform`, `hostPlatform`, and `targetPlatform` accurately.

::: {.callout-note}
This chapter completes **Part 6: Packaging Craft**. While previous chapters focused on compiling for the native host platform, production platform engineering requires building software for distributed fleets of varied architectures—ARM64 cloud servers (AWS Graviton, Ampere), embedded boards (Raspberry Pi), and edge gateways.
:::

## The Cross-Compilation Problem: Why Emulation Fails

Traditional CI/CD pipelines build multi-architecture binaries using QEMU user emulation (`binfmt_misc`):

```text
x86_64 CI Runner ──> [QEMU Software Translation] ──> Emulated aarch64 gcc / cargo
```

While emulation is conceptually simple, it incurs severe penalties:
1. **Extreme Performance Penalty:** Emulating an ARM64 instruction set on an x86_64 CPU slows execution down by **5x to 20x**. Large C++ or Rust codebases that compile in 5 minutes natively take over an hour under QEMU.
2. **Emulation Instability:** QEMU user-mode frequently crashes on complex multithreaded compilers, memory barriers, or signal handlers.
3. **Wasted Cloud Compute:** Engineering organizations burn thousands of dollars in CI compute hours waiting for emulated compilers to finish.

**The Solution:** True **cross-compilation**. An x86_64 compiler binary runs natively at full x86_64 hardware speed while emitting machine code targeted for ARM64 or RISC-V.

---

## The Nixpkgs Platform Model: Triples and System Types

Nixpkgs implements a rigorous, formalized model of cross-compilation based on the GNU toolchain conventions. Every derivation is evaluated in the context of three platforms:

| Platform Concept | Nix Attribute | Definition | Practical Meaning |
|------------------|---------------|------------|-------------------|
| **Build Platform** | `stdenv.buildPlatform` | The platform where compilation executes | The CPU and OS running `gcc`, `rustc`, or `go` (e.g. `x86_64-linux`) |
| **Host Platform** | `stdenv.hostPlatform` | The platform where the built package will run | The machine where the resulting application binary executes (e.g. `aarch64-linux`) |
| **Target Platform** | `stdenv.targetPlatform` | The platform for which a compiler generates code | Only relevant when building compilers (e.g. building an ARM64-targeted compiler) |

```text
Build Platform: x86_64-linux (Your laptop / CI Runner)
       │
       ▼ [Cross-Compiler runs at native x86_64 speed]
Host Platform:  aarch64-linux (Your AWS Graviton or Raspberry Pi server)
```

In standard native builds, `buildPlatform == hostPlatform`. In cross-compilation, `buildPlatform != hostPlatform`.

---

## Instant Cross-Toolchains with `pkgsCross`

Nixpkgs includes pre-configured cross-compilation package sets under `pkgsCross`. You do not need to compile a custom cross-toolchain from scratch; Nix provides them out of the box:

```bash
# Query available cross sets in the REPL
nix repl '<nixpkgs>'
nix-repl> builtins.attrNames pkgsCross
[ "aarch64-multiplatform" "armv7l-hf-multiplatform" "ppc64le" "riscv64" "x86_64-embedded" ... ]
```

To cross-compile any existing package from Nixpkgs for ARM64:

```bash
# Cross-compile GNU Hello from x86_64 to aarch64
nix build nixpkgs#pkgsCross.aarch64-multiplatform.hello

# Verify the resulting ELF binary architecture
file ./result/bin/hello
# Output: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, ARM a-arch64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked ...
```

Notice that `hello` was built without executing a single ARM instruction on your machine.

---

## Classifying Inputs: `nativeBuildInputs` vs `buildInputs`

The most critical rule in cross-compiling Nix derivations is placing dependencies in the correct input list:

| Input Attribute | Target Execution Platform | What Belongs Here |
|-----------------|---------------------------|-------------------|
| `nativeBuildInputs` | **Build Platform** (`buildPlatform`) | Compilers, code generators, build systems (`cmake`, `pkg-config`, `bison`, `protobuf`, `cargo`) |
| `buildInputs` | **Host Platform** (`hostPlatform`) | Libraries and headers that the binary links against (`openssl`, `glibc`, `zlib`, `sqlite`) |
| `depsBuildBuild` | **Build Platform** (`buildPlatform`) | Tools required to build tools for the build platform |

If you accidentally place `pkg-config` in `buildInputs`, Nix will attempt to run an ARM64 binary on your x86_64 machine, crashing with `Exec format error`.

## Language Ecosystems in Cross-Compilation

### 1. Cross-Compiling C/C++ Projects (CMake)

When using `stdenv` with `cmake`, Nixpkgs automatically generates a CMake toolchain file configured with the target triple:

```nix
# packages/my-c-service/default.nix
{ stdenv, lib, fetchFromGitHub, cmake, pkg-config, openssl, zlib }:

stdenv.mkDerivation rec {
  pname = "sensor-service";
  version = "1.2.0";

  src = fetchFromGitHub {
    owner = "example-corp";
    repo = pname;
    rev = "v${version}";
    hash = "sha256-AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=";
  };

  # Build-time tools running on the builder CPU
  nativeBuildInputs = [ cmake pkg-config ];

  # Target libraries for ARM64
  buildInputs = [ openssl zlib ];

  # CMake automatically receives CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME and CMAKE_C_COMPILER
  meta = with lib; {
    description = "C++ sensor processing service";
    platforms = platforms.linux;
  };
}
```

### 2. Cross-Compiling Rust with Cargo

`rustPlatform.buildRustPackage` natively supports cross-compilation when invoked from `pkgsCross`:

```nix
# packages/rust-service/default.nix
{ lib, rustPlatform, fetchFromGitHub, pkg-config, openssl }:

rustPlatform.buildRustPackage rec {
  pname = "telemetry-agent";
  version = "0.4.1";

  src = fetchFromGitHub {
    owner = "example-corp";
    repo = pname;
    rev = "v${version}";
    hash = "sha256-BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB=";
  };

  cargoHash = "sha256-CCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC=";

  nativeBuildInputs = [ pkg-config ];
  buildInputs = [ openssl ];

  # Disable tests during cross-compilation (since host binaries cannot run on build machine)
  doCheck = false;
}
```

Building this via `nix build .#pkgsCross.aarch64-multiplatform.telemetry-agent` uses an x86_64 `rustc` with `--target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` and cross-compiles OpenSSL cleanly.

### 3. Cross-Compiling Go Modules

Go has native cross-compilation built into its compiler via `GOOS` and `GOARCH`. `buildGoModule` handles this seamlessly:

```nix
# packages/go-api/default.nix
{ lib, buildGoModule, fetchFromGitHub }:

buildGoModule rec {
  pname = "gateway-api";
  version = "2.1.0";

  src = fetchFromGitHub {
    owner = "example-corp";
    repo = pname;
    rev = "v${version}";
    hash = "sha256-DDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD=";
  };

  vendorHash = "sha256-EEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE=";

  # If CGO is required, ensure cross-gcc is used
  CGO_ENABLED = 0; # Pure Go cross-compiles instantly

  doCheck = false;
}
```

## Flake Pattern for Multi-Architecture Outputs

Here is how to expose cross-compiled packages in your `flake.nix`:

```nix
{
  description = "Multi-Architecture Cross-Compilation Flake";

  inputs = {
    nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-26.05";
  };

  outputs = { self, nixpkgs }:
    let
      # Build platform is x86_64-linux
      pkgsNative = import nixpkgs { system = "x86_64-linux"; };
      
      # Cross package sets
      pkgsCrossAarch64 = import nixpkgs {
        system = "x86_64-linux";
        crossSystem = { config = "aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu"; };
      };

      pkgsCrossRiscv64 = import nixpkgs {
        system = "x86_64-linux";
        crossSystem = { config = "riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu"; };
      };
    in {
      packages.x86_64-linux = {
        # Native build
        default = pkgsNative.callPackage ./packages/my-service.nix {};

        # Cross-compiled builds for ARM64 and RISC-V
        arm64 = pkgsCrossAarch64.callPackage ./packages/my-service.nix {};
        riscv = pkgsCrossRiscv64.callPackage ./packages/my-service.nix {};
      };
    };
}
```

Now, from an x86_64 laptop or CI server, simply run:
```bash
nix build .#arm64
nix build .#riscv
```

## Common Cross-Compilation Pitfalls

| Failure Symptom | Root Cause | Fix |
|-----------------|------------|-----|
| `Exec format error` during build | A host-architecture binary was executed on the build machine (e.g. running unit tests or a code generator) | Set `doCheck = false;` during cross builds. Ensure code generators are placed in `nativeBuildInputs`. |
| `Cannot find -lssl` | Dynamic library placed in `nativeBuildInputs` instead of `buildInputs` | Move libraries the application links with into `buildInputs`. |
| `pkg-config` outputs host paths | Using host `pkg-config` instead of target cross-wrapper | Always pull `pkg-config` from `nativeBuildInputs`; Nix provides the target-prefixed wrapper (e.g. `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu-pkg-config`). |

## Checkpoint

- [ ] Cross-compiled a binary using `pkgsCross.aarch64-multiplatform` without running QEMU.
- [ ] Correctly separated host libraries in `buildInputs` from build tools in `nativeBuildInputs`.
- [ ] Exported multi-architecture cross builds cleanly in `flake.nix`.
